queue.tree_name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the Amalienburg
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by leaves shredded into narrow ribbons, with the odd branch reverting to ordinary broad beech leaves, standing alone at a path fork. It stands about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, Schlosspark Nymphenburg.
queue.story: No fern-leaved beech anywhere is much more than two centuries old, because the tree did not exist before about 1804. It is a cultivated form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow ribbons, and it cannot be relied on to come true from seed, so every one of them has been grafted or struck from cuttings taken off another. That gives this specimen an unusually hard ceiling on its age, which is useful in a park where almost nothing else has a date. It stands alone at a fork in the path about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, the rococo hunting lodge Francois de Cuvillies built in the 1730s, with a small metal plate on the trunk marking it as a natural monument. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its several separate stems, once a single trunk that split apart from the 1770s onward, now ringed by a low wall built in 1785 to stop souvenir-taking. It stands inside Fortingall churchyard.
queue.story:
In 2015 a tree that had been male for as long as anyone had recorded it grew berries on a single branch. The Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh reported the change, and beyond the novelty it was proof that the Fortingall Yew is a working organism rather than a standing relic.

Its age is genuinely disputed and always will be. Forestry and Land Scotland says 5,000 years. Bevan-Jones, the standard academic reference on ancient yews, gives 2,000 to 3,000 and allows that the tree may only date from a post-Roman Christian site here, which would make it around 1,500. Nobody can settle it, because the heartwood rotted out centuries ago and there are no rings left to count.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the lone veteran oak on the grass beside the road. It stands beside Kentish Way, on the edge of The Glades shopping centre grounds.
queue.story:
When Bromley built The Glades shopping centre in the 1980s, this oak was reprieved. It now stands beside Kentish Way, a veteran on the grass at the edge of a mall that opened in 1991.

It was here long before any of that. The Bromley Civic Society says the oak first stood on the corner of the grounds of Bromley Lodge, where they met Love Lane.

How long it has stood there is disputed. The Civic Society calls it over 500 years old; the 2010 Time Out guide to the Great Trees of London says about 400. queue.tree_name: The Great Cedar of Kasuga Taisha
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the second tree growing from its base, reaching toward the neighbouring hall through a hole cut in the roof. It stands beside the Naoraiden, near Kasuga Taisha's inner gate.
queue.story: There is a picture scroll, donated to this shrine in 1309, in which this cedar appears as a sapling. Seven centuries later it is roughly eight metres around and twenty-five tall, standing beside the hall where offerings are shared after the rituals, and the sapling in the painting is the same organism. Almost no ancient tree anywhere can be checked against its own portrait as a young plant. The better story is what grows out of its base. A second tree, a shinpaku, took root there and grew toward the neighbouring hall, and rather than cut it back somebody cut a hole in the roof and let it through. The hall still has the hole. Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768 for the deity of the Fujiwara clan
queue.name: The Great Cedar of Kasuga Taisha
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better

queue.recognise: A hard-twisted trunk with limbs reading as outstretched arms under a coat of moss. Nothing on the ground names it and there is no path to it, so the pin marks the grove rather than the tree.
queue.story:
The grove these trees belong to was already standing when the Portuguese found Madeira uninhabited in 1419. Fanal is a protected 20-hectare nucleus of til, Ocotea foetens, on the Paul da Serra plateau inside the UNESCO laurel forest, and the island's register dates it only as centenas de anos, hundreds of years, referencing a stand that predates settlement. The eight trunks the surveyors measured run from 0.68 to 2.28 metres round.

queue.recognise: The huge fig with a car-parts sculpture of Atlas appearing to hold up one long branch, a few metres from the Recoleta Cemetery gate.
queue.story: One branch of this fig reaches thirty metres out from the trunk and is over a metre thick where it leaves it. Since 2014 a sculpture of Atlas, welded from car parts by the Uruguayan artist Joaquin Arbiza Brianza, has stood underneath it appearing to take the weight. The city government calls this the oldest tree in Buenos Aires, and nobody agrees on how it got here. One account has the Recoleto friars planting it around 1718. Another credits the agronomist Martin Jose de Altolaguirre, who kept an orchard of exotic species on this ground around 1781.
